utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things about witnesses. The first thing, please, in private session, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of the Chamber's ruling on the financial expert Morten Torkildsen and in light of the necessary timetable problems we face from time to time, we would ask that the accused and the amici be ready to deal with Morten Torkildsen at short notice at any time after this week. He, like Graham Blewitt, can then be a witness who can fill time should for any reason time suddenly become available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And so that the accused could follow this, Torkildsen's report, Mr. Torkildsen's first report, was not admitted. That was the Kosovo one. But the Bosnia and Croatian one, the second report, was admitted, save for the book. Yes. Well, let us move on as quickly as we can, except for this: Mr. Nice, at some stage this week we should address the various concerns raised by the Prosecution in relation to witnesses and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be right to do that at a time during the week when we can fit in a period for procedural matters, also to deal with some of the Croatia 92 bis witnesses also. It may be if you would have in mind the matters you want us to address so we can be in a position to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And of course it would be a helpful time now because the Chamber's decisions about 92 bis give us a pattern of probable rulings for the future that enable us the better to understand the problems we face. Thank you very much. May we go into closed session, then, for this witness, and for those viewing in the public gallery, my learned friend Mr. Groome's expectation is that the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, the accused may want to raise something. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone. We didn't hear the beginning of that. The interpreters apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They didn't catch what you said, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I would like to make certain requests before we go on to the witness, and the first of them is this: I ask that you enable me to be heard with respect to a media campaign unprecedented thus far which is being waged in Belgrade. It started just before the weekend under conditions of complete lawlessness and terror exercised by the authorities there, and it is being waged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only matters we have to deal with are those in connection with this trial, and at the moment I can see nothing in relation to this trial in what you're saying. Now, you -- if you are concerned -- if it was your concern that it may in some way prejudice the Trial Chamber, you need set your mind at rest on that score. There is no consideration given and not much read of what is said in the press. So we try this case on the facts. Now, if there is some relation in what you're saying to the trial, then you can raise it. Otherwise, as you know, it's not a matter that we can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does have to do with this trial, Mr. May, and that is why I consider that you're duty-bound to hear me, because I also consider, and I shall insist upon this, that the link be established between the activities of that so-called Prosecution over there and the media campaign and accusations being hurled through that media campaign and being waged in these past few days. They're being waged against my wife and myself in a way to place this via the media and accuse me, try me, and judge me. It is not a legal proceedings, it is a media proceedings. And the best evidence of this is that they haven't come to question me at all, although they said this loud and clear, that they would do so. And your porte-parole has said, as far as I was able to see -- he made a statement on television, actually, and said that it was being made possible for them to come here, to appear here, and to interrogate me. They know full well that I had the power and authority and not my wife, but they did not come and contact me, but they have launched their efforts against my wife which is best proof that they are not actually interested in any kind of investigation, but they are waging --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The matters we can deal with are those, as I've told you, concerned with this trial, and matters concerning your wife are not matters with which this trial is concerned. I'm going to consult a moment as to whether we need to hear you any further on this topic. What is the connection that you allege between the Prosecution? If there is a word in this of coherence, we will listen to it, but at the moment it's simply a wild allegation of some sort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I consider, and I'm going to prove this, that the revenge against my wife and against my children is being launched because of me and the struggle that I am waging here, and I claim that it was orchestrated with this illegal Prosecution over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, we're not going to hear any more of this. It's to do with a speech that you're making about Belgrade. It has nothing to do with this trial. We will go into -- we will go into closed session to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please could you bear in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. If there is a further point, in due course we will hear it, but none today. We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust the Chamber has the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust the Chamber has the summary evidence of the next witness, Mr. Gusalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we have. It's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The table on the front of the witness, as His Honour Judge Kwon made reference to in respect of the last witness, a footnote should perhaps be, not disregarded but viewed with caution both as to whether exhibits are produced for identification or to be tendered and as to whether it would be necessary for other evidence to always to authenticate documents. The policy of the Chamber, of course, is to take documents as accepted unless otherwise challenged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that we're in open session again and the new witness hasn't been brought in to the courtroom yet, may I have the floor with respect to my request, the request which I wish to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me reiterate that I ask you to enable me to be heard and to be questioned publicly with respect to the media campaign that is being waged publicly too, because revenge against my wife and child come -- date back to the worst years of the last century. And I should also like to have investigated the involvement of this illegal Prosecution into the fabrication of untruths that are being launched. Apart from that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, I've stopped you before. Events in Belgrade are not a matter for this Tribunal. If it has any direct impingement on this trial, we'll of course deal with it. But it -- nothing you've said shows that it does. Now, I thought you wanted to say something about your health. That we will listen to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you about my health, but it does have direct bearing. It is the desire to make it impossible for my wife to lend me support and assistance. And in addition to that, I wish to inform you that several members of the national committee have been taken into custody, the committee for the defence of my liberties, although they have no grounds for doing so. Therefore, it is an orchestrated endeavour to exert pressure upon me and my family because this false indictment is undergoing a fiasco here every day. And I consider it to be your duty to establish the degree to which they are involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is matter of comment by you. There's absolutely no evidence to support what you're saying. There may well be reasons why people have been arrested. But at the moment, we're not going to act on that sort of allegation. Now, do you want to say something about your health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards my health; I have received these papers, the documents you discussed in my absence last Tuesday, and my first objection is the following, that you should be discussing me in my absence. That's my first objection. And secondly, in this piece of paper it says, and I'm going to quote, "noting the reported refusal of the accused [In English] to take the prescribed increased medication recommended by cardiologist Dr. Dijkman." [Interpretation] In your discussions here, you have created the impression that I refused to take my medication and that thereby I intentionally made my health worse, which is a complete lie. I have discussed this with the head of the detention centre and the sole employed medical employee of the prison. The fact is that I never refused to take my medications. Every medication prescribed to me I did take. Now, the fact that I indicated, I pointed out the highly negative aftereffects that the medication was having, the medication I was taking, and asked that the medication be replaced by a better medication, was a normal conversation between physician and patient. And I think it is the right of the doctor and the patient's right to indicate this. I have received information, references, that the medication, the particular drug which was given to me to reduce my blood pressure caused, among other side-effects, two very serious side-effects, the symptoms of which I have been feeling for some time on myself. One of them is drowsiness and the other is insomnia. You will admit, gentlemen, that drowsiness means that I will have to invest additional efforts, additional involvement, and it will be additionally fatiguing to me to undertake the job I'm doing here. And that insomnia, on other hand, makes it impossible for me to have the rest I need, the minimum amount of rest I need. So I pointed this out, and I have received the references that I table here. They are references by world professional institutions that indicate the effects of the side-effects. So you discussed this subject here, and you discussed it as if I was refusing to take my medications. The very day that you had this discussion and assumed the positions you did that were quite wrong, Dr. Dijkman, bearing all this in mind, the side-effects, changed my therapy. And the day after my therapy was changed, I had a whole night's sleep, which shows that he was right, that it was right for him to give me other medication, and the fact that your discussions here to the effect that I refused to take my medications was completely unfounded, and it was ill-intentioned and interpreted by Mr. Nice in an ill-intentioned way. I have here a letter from my own physician. It is signed, and it says that I suffer from dizziness, drowsiness, and insomnia. And he also told me that we can send this to Houston and that they will confirm that it is all correct. But you need no better confirmation than the fact that as of last Tuesday, that is the very day that you were discussing my health here, my therapy was changed and my blood pressure has been brought down to the normal level two days later and I have been sleeping normally. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I have slept normally immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good, Mr. Milosevic. Keep taking the medication. If you're not present at any stage, it may be necessary for the Court to consider your position on the basis of the reports which it has received. It has nothing to do with Mr. Nice. He made no interpretation and cannot be criticised for it. Now, keep taking the medication and we'll be able to get on. If you don't turn up, it may be necessary for the Court, in exceptional circumstances, to discuss the progress of the trial without you, you not being here to contribute. But we don't go on without you at the moment. Now, let us get on with the trial. Now, what? Yes. Yes, you made --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my comment and objection -- Mr. May, my objection was such that it referred to you too because you were the one that drew the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Mr. Nice's ill-intentioned interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right. On the basis of the reports which we received. Now, we act on those reports and those are what we received. Now, we're not going to take this any further. You're now recovered, and as we say, you should keep taking the medication. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Milosevic. We've heard your views. You've made your objection and you've been told what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Alija Gusalic. While he's coming in, I remind the Court that I never respond to the various allegations that are made by the accused. I'm not going to change the policy now. If at any time the Chamber thinks that these allegations may be simply for external consumption, it's always possible to redact the transcript. I'm not going to enter into any kind of a debate with the accused over that sort of allegation. I should say, in relation to Alija Gusalic, that Exhibit number 2 is an exhibit, a video that I will not be producing at all and will not be relying on. To some degree I've served it, or I've left it on the list because, depending on what challenges are made, it could or part of it could become material in re-examination and I can remember an earlier occasion when I think Mr. Saxon was examining a witness where something was available for re-examination and the Chamber was concerned that it hadn't been, in the vernacular, flagged up in advance. So there's just the possibility that it may turn up in that way, but to save time, I'm not going to use it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter from the amici. I was going to raise this issue. I think we're talking about tab 2. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It probably is tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the video and its transcript. My guess is that's true. The interview with Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it's tab 2 in the folders we've been given, Your Honours. I was going to raise a matter at an appropriate moment concerning it. It seems to be in two parts. There seems to be an interview with Seselj included, which confused me even more about it, but I think it's been withdraw. We can probably take it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your full name Alija Gusalic, were you born in Zvornik, moving to Bijeljina as a child, first marrying a Serbian woman by whom you had two children?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will of course find the relevant towns shown on page 29 of the atlas, if that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the conflict began, Mr. Gusalic, or the time of the conflict began, did Muslims by and large live in the centre of Bijeljina with the Serbs living in the suburbs and surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Generally, had relations between Muslims and Serbs been good or bad?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Generally good at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at that time, were key positions, such as the mayor and commander of the police, held by Serbs or by Muslims or by a combination?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Predominantly by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few months - two or three - before the conflict in Bijeljina, were letters sent out by the Territorial Defence for reservists?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were any Muslims called up as reservists?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had served ten months in the JNA, and I think neither you nor any of your brothers were called up. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although two of your brothers were later to serve at the front line with Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They were forced to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic, head of the Serbian Radical Party in Bijeljina, let's deal with him. Did the man Seselj visit Bijeljina before the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mirko Blagojevic become the leader of the local Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Semberija.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could move a little closer to the microphone, please. Was the man Blagojevic what was known as a duke?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did Serb Radical Party members, particularly members who were bearded, come from Serbia to see Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did he take over or set up some kind of a base in a cafe that was to be known as the Cafe Srbija?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Arkan's men and Seselj's men, did they appear in the area and based at Amajlije, which is on the map immediately south-east of Bijeljina, about 4 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a training base or was there a training base there that they used?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, like a camp where they underwent training for Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Roughly how many Arkan's men and roughly how many Seselj's men there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to give you an exact figure, but there were more than a hundred Arkan's men and probably as many Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these two groups distinguishable by their appearance, please?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes, Arkan's men were well dressed, whereas Seselj's men wore beards and cockades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did tensions grow and were those growing tensions reflected in the restricted use of the Cafe Srbija?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Of course it was hard. People who went there continued going there, only Serbs. The Muslims couldn't go there. They held their meetings there for the attack on Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other microphone be switch on as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the months prior to the conflict in Bijeljina, had there been distribution of arms to Serb men?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By whom were the Serb Radical Party Serbian men armed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Seselj take any part in this or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Of course he did. That's where they held their meetings. Seselj was the boss, and Seselj instructed Mirko Blagojevic to distribute the weapons, and he organised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were Serb members of the SDS also armed; and if so, by whom or from where?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Of course they were armed. In the Bijeljina garrison where the regular Yugoslav People's Army was. They armed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence weapons being used to arm those men, yes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Muslims have some weapons, including hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mostly hunting rifles, in fact. And if someone could afford to buy a weapon, again they would buy them from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will go on until ten to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Mauzer, was he somebody you knew from before the conflict or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Not personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he have his own unit?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Comprised of what sort of men and known as what?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mostly young Serbs were there. They were very well-armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the name of the group?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mauzer's men, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You can't remember any other name by which they went, any other animal title? If it comes back to you, let us know. Of what group or brigade had Mauzer originally been a member?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Maybe later on. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The Cafe Istanbul, was that opened about a month before the war started, it being owned by a man named Goga?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: That was his nickname. I don't know his real name, but otherwise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it initially visited by both Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it about 50 metres apart from Cafe Srbija and did it serve as a sort of meeting place for members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: No one met there. Both Serbs and Muslims and Croats went to that cafe. All the people went there. Maybe the distance was 50 or 60 metres. I don't know exactly. But they were very close to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an incident on the 29th of March at the Cafe Istanbul? Who did what, and how many people were injured as a result?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Seven people were injured. A grenade was thrown in there. I think the man's name was Goran from Borovo. Among the seven, I think there were three Serbs that were hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you visit the Cafe Srbija the following day on your horse?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a beer there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mirko Blagojevic say something to you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I asked for another beer, and he said he wouldn't give me any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which year are we in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't established that. Also, the witness was on a horse?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On a horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Riding on a horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Riding on a horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid the story has not got a happy ending for the horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you return to the Cafe Istanbul and did you speak to Goga and a man known as Cosa?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you provided with a hand grenade?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you return to the Cafe Srbija with the hand grenade, on your horse?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe 20 or 10 metres in front of the Srbija cafe. That is as far as I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to you and indeed to your horse?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I was hit and the horse was hit too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, what ultimately happened to the horse? The horse died, I think.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I never found him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it your intention to throw the grenade or was your intention less than that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I hadn't really intended to throw the grenade, but in those days, when I went to that cafe, there were only soldiers there, no civilians, and now I regret that I didn't throw that grenade in view of what they did afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a result of what they did to you as you approached on your horse, were you injured?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Later on, I was injured and the horse was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. How were you injured?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: They shot at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as a result of that, did you go to hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which, when you got there, was in the hands of Muslims, being taken over by Serbs a couple of days later?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the hospital while you were there, did members of one of the groups you've spoken of enter the hospital, inquiring if there were any "balijas" there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which group of men were these two men from?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic's Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. My mistake. Was there any -- or my question not being as helpful as it might have been. Do you remember members of one of the armed units coming in and making any inquiry about balijas?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: This was before Mirko. Two guys came in. They were looking for balijas. I managed to lie and say that my name was Dragan, and they left. I think they were Arkan's men. After them, Mirko Blagojevic came with another two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did those men do to you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did those men, the two men with Mirko Blagojevic, do to you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: I had an infusion. I had bandages on me. He tore off the injection. He hit me with his butt. He threw me to the ground. He stabbed me with a bayonet in the leg, and they said if anyone was taken to Amajlije they were either slaughtered or tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This incident ended with Blagojevic giving what instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have some water? Can I take a drink?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, do, please. And, Mr. Nice, it's almost time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can see if the witness can help us with this last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Gusalic, was this: That the incident you described where Blagojevic visited you and his men attacked you, ended with Blagojevic giving what instructions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA GUSALIC
utterances.text: He said that he would leave me there and that he would come back for me when they captured the hospital, to take me to the village of Amajlije for them to take it out on me before I die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If that's a suitable moment. Mr. Gusalic, we're going to adjourn your evidence until tomorrow morning. Could you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow to continue it. And meanwhile, could you remember not to speak to anybody about it until your evidence is over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Before we adjourn, I'm just going to announce the numbers of the witnesses whose evidence under Rule 92 bis we're going to consider later in the week, so that preparations can be made. The numbers are: C-1052, 1063, 1084, 1091, 1140, 1152, 1153, 1168, 1187, 1203, 1230, 1231, 1232, 1234. We will adjourn now until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of April, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.57 p.m.,
